Having finished discussing the main parameters we use in describing vowels of a Ghanaian 
language, there is a fourth parameter as mentioned earlier in this sub-strand which is not 
common among Ghanaian languages. This parameter is advancement of the tongue.

Advancement of the tongue root (ATR) 
(Please, discuss only if applicable in your language)
This parameter, which is prominent in a few Ghanaian languages including Akan, Dagbani, 
etc. It is used to determine the position the tongue root assumes when a vowel is being 
produced. By this parameter, we try to find out if there is tension or pressure on the tongue 
or not during production of vowels. When a vowel is produced with pressure on the tongue 
thereby causing the tongue root to draw back, we say that vowel is produced with Advanced 
Tongue Root (ATR) i.e. (+ATR) vowels. When vowels are produced with the tongue root in 
its natural neutral position, we label those vowels are Unadvanced Tongue Root i.e. (-ATR) 
vowels. Some examples of (+ATR) vowels are: /i, e, u, o/, and examples of (-ATR) vowels 
are /ɪ, ɛ, ɔ/.

The concept of consonant
As was mentioned earlier in the section, consonant is another type of speech sounds apart 
from vowel. The concept consonant refers to a speech sound in which during production the 
breath, which we have termed airflow, is at least obstructed. Based on this explanation, we 
can contrast vowel and consonant by saying that while in the production of vowel there is 
very minimal or no obstruction of airflow, there is significant obstruction of airflow when 
producing consonants. We combined vowels and consonants form a word.
Description of consonants
When we want to describe a consonant, there are parameters that are used for that purpose. 
The three parameters used to describe consonants are: place of articulation manner of 
articulation, and voicing. We will discuss each of the three parameters and provide examples 
to illustrate it.
7

Place of articulation
This refers to a point of contact between two organs of speech during production of 
consonant sounds. As was observed in the video on speech sounds, some of the places of 
articulation in a Ghanaian language are bilabial, labio-dental, alveolar, palatal, velar, etc. 
The following are some places of articulation and the consonants of a Ghanaian language 
that are produced in these places.
• Bilabial: In producing bilabial sounds, we bring our two lips closely together. For 
example, /p, b, m/.
• Alveolar: When producing an alveolar sound, we bring our front part of the 
tongue to the hard palate. Some examples of alveolar sounds are /t, d, s, n/.
• Labio-dental: Labio-dental sounds are produced by touching your upper set of 
the teeth with your lower lip. For example, /f/.
• Palatal: In producing palatal sounds, we raise the centre of our tongue towards 
the hard palate. An example of palatal sound is /j/.
• Velar: When producing velar sounds, we push the back of our tongue towards the 
velum or the soft palate. Some examples of velar sounds are /k, g/.

Manner of articulation
This refers to how the airflow is obstructed in the course of production of consonant 
sounds. There are degrees of obstruction of airflow during speech sounds production. For 
example, in some consonants, in their production there is a momentary complete blocking 
or obstruction and sudden release of airflow. Based on the degree of closure or obstruction, 
some manners of articulation can be identified with consonants of a Ghanaian language. the 
articulators configure and interact during the production of speech sound. Some examples 
of manners of articulation of consonants include stops, fricatives, affricate, nasal, lateral, 
etc. The following are some manners of articulation and examples of consonant sounds of 
a Ghanaian language produced in those manners.
• Stops: As the name suggests, in producing stop sounds, the continuous airflow is 
completely stopped or obstructed momentarily or briefly. The obstructed airflow 
is released suddenly. For example, /p, b, t, d, k, g, m, n/. Based on where the 
trapped or obstructed airflow is released from, we can categorize stop sounds into 
two, namely oral stop and nasal stop. When the trapped air is released through the 
mouth, it is known as plosive, e.g. /p, b, t, d, k, g/. On the other hand, when the 
trapped air is released through the nose, it is known as nasal stop, e.g. /m, n/.
• Fricative: For the production of fricative, there is no complete obstruction 
of airflow but rather a narrow space so that airflow passes through the space 
gradually thereby causing friction. Some examples of fricative sounds are /f, s/.

• Affricate: In producing affricate sounds, there are two stages involved; first there 
is a complete obstruction of airflow, and in the final stages the obstructed airflow

a Ghanaian language.
• Lateral: In the production of lateral sound, the front part of the tongue will touch

example of a trill sound is /r/.

My dear learner, the third parameter we use in describing consonant sounds is the voicing.

glottis assumes two states; either it is vibrating or it is not vibrating. When the vocal folds are 
vibrating, the sounds we produce are known as voiced consonants. On the other hand, when 
the vocal folds are not vibrating when articulating consonant sounds we call those consonant 
sounds voiceless sounds. Some examples of voiced consonants include /g/, /d/, /m/, /b/, and 
voiceless consonants include /f/, /s/, /k/, /t/, / ʃ/, etc.

Phonology (Speech sounds of a Ghanaian language)
INTRODUCTION
Dear learner, you are welcome to this section which discusses the foundation of language 
(speech sounds). You will be introduced to the concepts of vowels and consonants of your 
language of study and how speech sounds are described (parameter). It will focus on where 
the speech sounds occur in words of a Ghanaian language. For example, where vowels and 
consonants can occur in a word of a Ghanaian language such as initial position, medial 
position, or final position of a word. Again, Dear learner you will be introduced to the 
distribution of vowels and consonants in your language, aiding you to form meaningful 
words and facilitate effective speaking and reading in the language. This section is essential 
for learners not only in the context of Ghanaian language studies but also to establish links 
with related subjects such as English and other languages. This section equips you with 
foundational knowledge and functional understanding of speech sounds and their role in 
language learning. In summary, you should be able to identify, explain, produce, and label 
vowel charts and consonant tables of your language of study.
At the end of this section, you should be able to:
1. Describe the vowels of a Ghanaian language using the right parameters (e.g., lip posture, 
tongue height and part of the tongue).
2. Describe the consonants of the Ghanaian language using the right parameters (e.g., voicing, 
place of articulation and manner of articulation).
3. Explain the distribution of vowels of the Ghanaian language (e.g., word initial, medial and 
final).
4. Explain the distribution of consonants of the Ghanaian language (e.g., word initial, medial 
and final).
Key ideas
•	 Production refers to the making or saying of a speech sound in language. Speech 
sound is a sound used in the formation of words for human communication. The 
production of speech sound involves obstruction which is the interruption of free 
flow of air during production of speech sounds. Sounds are distributed in languages 
and this refers to the place or position in a word where a sound can appear. Sound 
involves airflow which is a mass movement of air that is meant for the production of 
speech sounds. Another term for it is airstream.

Year 1
Types of speech sounds
Speech sounds can be grouped into two main types, namely vowels and consonants. It is the 
combination of these two types of sounds that produces words. In other words, all words 
are made up of individual speech sounds. For examples, the word pan consists of three 
individual speech sounds, that is, /p/, /a/, /n/. The sound /a/ is a vowel, whereas the sounds 
/p/ and /n/ are consonants. In the following topics we discuss both vowels and consonants 
focusing on how each is produced in a Ghanaian language.
The concept of vowel
The concept vowel  refers as a speech sound in which production there is a little or no 
obstruction of the flow of air in the oral cavity. In other words, a speech sound which when 
being produced the air is not obstructed or it is minimally obstructed in the oral cavity is 
referred to as a vowel. Since in their production there is no or very little obstruction of 
airflow, vowels are comparatively heard louder when they are produced. Vowels are very 
important part of words. There cannot be a word without a vowel or vowel-like sound. This 
important role vowel plays in a word will later on in your second year be discussed when 
we are talking about the syllable.
Description of vowels
Dear learner, in describing vowels of a Ghanaian language, there are certain properties 
we use. These properties are often termed parameters. Parameters simply refer to the 
characteristics that a vowel possesses. The main parameters used in describing vowels are 
the tongue height, lip posture, and part of the tongue used during the production of the 
vowel sound. In addition to the three, there is a fourth parameter called advancement of 
the tongue root in some Ghanaian languages such as Akan. Let us begin the discussions of 
these parameters.
Lip position/posture
The parameter lip posture is used to determine the position your lips assume when you are 
producing a vowel. So, at this level, the lips assume two main postures or positions, namely 
rounded or unrounded. That is, whether the lips are rounded or they are not rounded when a 
vowel sound is being produced. Based on this posture of the lips, we can divide vowels of a 
Ghanaian language into two, namely ‘rounded’ and ‘spread/unrounded.’ Some examples 
of rounded vowels are /u, o, ɔ/. examples of unrounded vowels, on the other hand, are /i, e, 
a/.

Tongue height/Height of the tongue
This refers to the position of the tongue in reference to the root of the mouth when producing 
vowel sounds. It is assumed that when we are producing vowels, the mouth opens when we 
drop the jaw. This can be high, mid, or low. When we drop our jaws to the lowest possible 
position, the vowels produced in this way are referred to as low vowels. Examples of low 
vowel is /a/, and in some Ghanaian languages [æ]. When we open our mouth wide enough 
but not as low as when producing low vowels, then the vowels we produced are termed mid 
vowels. Some examples of mid vowels in a Ghanaian language are /e, o/. In producing high 
vowels, on the other hand, the mouth is significantly opened but not as wide as mid vowels, 
thereby allowing enough air to flow through the oral cavity. Some examples of high vowels 
in a Ghanaian language are /i, u/.
Activity 1.2 
Begin practicing the production of vowels in your language of study focusing on how 
high or how low you raise your jaws or open your mouth.
Part of the tongue
This parameter refers to the area of the tongue where the vowel sound is produced. It is 
assumed that when we are producing vowels, some parts of the tongue move. We cannot 
easily feel this movement though. Three parts of the tongue are assumed to be involved 
when a vowel sounds is being produced. These parts are the front part, middle part, and 
back part. Based on that, the parameter gives us three classes of vowels, namely front, mid, 
and back vowels. In producing front vowels, it is the front part of the tongue that moves. 
Some examples of front vowels of a Ghanaian language are /i, e, ɛ/. For the production of 
mid vowels, the middle of the tongue is assumed to move. Therefore, the following vowel is 
an example of a mid-vowel: /a/. For back vowels, on the other hand, as the name suggests, it 
is the back of the tongue that is involved in their production. Some examples of back vowels 
of a Ghanaian language are: /u, o, ɔ/.
Activity 1.3 
Practice how to produce vowels of your language of study with focus on the part of 
the tongue.
Having finished discussing the main parameters we use in describing vowels of a Ghanaian 
language, there is a fourth parameter as mentioned earlier in this sub-strand which is not 
common among Ghanaian languages. This parameter is advancement of the tongue.

Advancement of the tongue root (ATR) 
(Please, discuss only if applicable in your language)
This parameter, which is prominent in a few Ghanaian languages including Akan, Dagbani, 
etc. It is used to determine the position the tongue root assumes when a vowel is being 
produced. By this parameter, we try to find out if there is tension or pressure on the tongue 
or not during production of vowels. When a vowel is produced with pressure on the tongue 
thereby causing the tongue root to draw back, we say that vowel is produced with Advanced 
Tongue Root (ATR) i.e. (+ATR) vowels. When vowels are produced with the tongue root in 
its natural neutral position, we label those vowels are Unadvanced Tongue Root i.e. (-ATR) 
vowels. Some examples of (+ATR) vowels are: /i, e, u, o/, and examples of (-ATR) vowels 
are /ɪ, ɛ, ɔ/.

the movement of your tongue root to distinguish advanced tongue roots (+ATR) from 
unadvanced tongue root (-ATR) vowels.

The concept of consonant
As was mentioned earlier in the section, consonant is another type of speech sounds apart 
from vowel. The concept consonant refers to a speech sound in which during production the 
breath, which we have termed airflow, is at least obstructed. Based on this explanation, we 
can contrast vowel and consonant by saying that while in the production of vowel there is 
very minimal or no obstruction of airflow, there is significant obstruction of airflow when 
producing consonants. We combined vowels and consonants form a word.
Description of consonants
When we want to describe a consonant, there are parameters that are used for that purpose. 
The three parameters used to describe consonants are: place of articulation manner of 
articulation, and voicing. We will discuss each of the three parameters and provide examples 
to illustrate it.
7

Year 1
Place of articulation
This refers to a point of contact between two organs of speech during production of 
consonant sounds. As was observed in the video on speech sounds, some of the places of 
articulation in a Ghanaian language are bilabial, labio-dental, alveolar, palatal, velar, etc. 
The following are some places of articulation and the consonants of a Ghanaian language 
that are produced in these places.
• Bilabial: In producing bilabial sounds, we bring our two lips closely together. For 
example, /p, b, m/.
• Alveolar: When producing an alveolar sound, we bring our front part of the 
tongue to the hard palate. Some examples of alveolar sounds are /t, d, s, n/.
• Labio-dental: Labio-dental sounds are produced by touching your upper set of 
the teeth with your lower lip. For example, /f/.
• Palatal: In producing palatal sounds, we raise the centre of our tongue towards 
the hard palate. An example of palatal sound is /j/.
• Velar: When producing velar sounds, we push the back of our tongue towards the 
velum or the soft palate. Some examples of velar sounds are /k, g/.

Provide examples of Ghanaian languages word that begins with each of the places of

Manner of articulation
This refers to how the airflow is obstructed in the course of production of consonant 
sounds. There are degrees of obstruction of airflow during speech sounds production. For 
example, in some consonants, in their production there is a momentary complete blocking 
or obstruction and sudden release of airflow. Based on the degree of closure or obstruction, 
some manners of articulation can be identified with consonants of a Ghanaian language. the 
articulators configure and interact during the production of speech sound. Some examples 
of manners of articulation of consonants include stops, fricatives, affricate, nasal, lateral, 
etc. The following are some manners of articulation and examples of consonant sounds of 
a Ghanaian language produced in those manners.
• Stops: As the name suggests, in producing stop sounds, the continuous airflow is 
completely stopped or obstructed momentarily or briefly. The obstructed airflow 
is released suddenly. For example, /p, b, t, d, k, g, m, n/. Based on where the 
trapped or obstructed airflow is released from, we can categorize stop sounds into 
two, namely oral stop and nasal stop. When the trapped air is released through the 
mouth, it is known as plosive, e.g. /p, b, t, d, k, g/. On the other hand, when the 
trapped air is released through the nose, it is known as nasal stop, e.g. /m, n/.
• Fricative: For the production of fricative, there is no complete obstruction 
of airflow but rather a narrow space so that airflow passes through the space 
gradually thereby causing friction. Some examples of fricative sounds are /f, s/.
8

• Affricate: In producing affricate sounds, there are two stages involved; first there 
is a complete obstruction of airflow, and in the final stages the obstructed airflow 
is released gradually (not suddenly). Some examples include /tʃ/ as applicable in 
a Ghanaian language.
• Lateral: In the production of lateral sound, the front part of the tongue will touch 
the alveolar ridge allowing airflow from only the side of the mouth. An example 
of a lateral sound is /l/.
• Trill: Trill sound is produced by the tongue, which is the active articulator, 
touching the passive articulator; the alveolar ridge in quick succession. An 
example of a trill sound is /r/.
Voicing
My dear learner, the third parameter we use in describing consonant sounds is the voicing. 
When we are making or producing consonant sounds, our vocal folds, which are inside our 
glottis assumes two states; either it is vibrating or it is not vibrating. When the vocal folds are 
vibrating, the sounds we produce are known as voiced consonants. On the other hand, when 
the vocal folds are not vibrating when articulating consonant sounds we call those consonant 
sounds voiceless sounds. Some examples of voiced consonants include /g/, /d/, /m/, /b/, and 
voiceless consonants include /f/, /s/, /k/, /t/, / ʃ/, etc.

Sound distribution
The concept sound distribution simply refers to the position in a word where speech sounds 
can occur in a language. Every language has some restrictions on where it can permit 
a speech sound to occur. The three positions that speech sounds can occur in word are 
initial position, medial position, or final positions. Let us begin our discussions with the 
distribution of vowels.
Vowel distribution
Vowel distribution simply refers to the position that a vowel can occur in a word in a 
Ghanaian language. When a vowel occurs at the beginning of a word, we say it has occurred 
in a word initial position. When it occurs at the middle of a word, we refer to that position 
as the word medial position, while when it occurs at the end of a word, it is referred to

distributions differently. It is also important to note that some of the vowels can occur in 
all the three positions in words in a language. Let us consider in the example below the

1. asɛm

say that /a/ can occur in word medial. In the third example, /a/ is the last sound that ends 
the word thus, /a/ can occur at word final.

Consonant distribution
The concept consonant distribution simply refers to the position in a word where a consonant 
can occur in a particular Ghanaian language. A consonant that occurs at the beginning of a 
word is referred to as word initial consonant. When a consonant occurs at the middle of a word, 
we refer to it as word medial consonant. When a consonant occurs at the end of a word, we 
refer to refer to it as word final consonant. Let us note that some consonants can occur in all 
positions of a word. For example, in some Ghanaian languages, the consonant /m/ can occur in 
the three positions in a word.

Some examples of mid vowels in a Ghanaian language are /e, o/. In producing 
high vowels, on the other hand, the mouth is significantly opened but not as wide 
as mid vowels, thereby allowing enough air to flow through the oral cavity. Some 
examples of high vowels in a Ghanaian language are /i, u/.

Part of the tongue:
This parametre refers to the area of the tongue where the vowel sound is produced. 
It is assumed that when we are producing vowels, some parts of the tongue 
move. We cannot easily feel this movement though. Three parts of the tongue 
are assumed to be involved when a vowel sounds is being produced. These parts 
5

are the front part, middle part, and back part. Based on that, the parametre gives 
us three classes of vowels, namely front, mid, and back vowels. In producing 
front vowels, it is the front part of the tongue that moves. Some examples of front 
vowels of a Ghanaian language are /i, e, ɛ/. For the production of mid vowels, 
the middle of the tongue is assumed to move. Therefore, the following vowel is 
an example of a mid-vowel: /a/. For back vowels, on the other hand, as the name 
suggests, it is the back of the tongue that is involved in their production. Some 
examples of back vowels of a Ghanaian language are: /u, o, ɔ/.

Having finished discussing the main parametres we use in describing vowels of 
a Ghanaian language, there is a fourth parametre as mentioned earlier in this 
sub-strand which is not common among Ghanaian languages. This parametre is 
advancement of the tongue.
Advancement of the tongue root (ATR): (Please, discuss only if 
applicable in your language)
This parametre, which is prominent in a few Ghanaian languages including Akan, 
Dagbani, etc. It is used to determine the position the tongue root assumes when a 
vowel is being produced. By this parametre, we try to find out if there is tension 
or pressure on the tongue or not during production of vowels. When a vowel is 
produced with pressure on the tongue thereby causing the tongue root to draw 
back, we say that vowel is produced with Advanced Tongue Root (ATR) i.e. 
(+ATR) vowels. When vowels are produced with the tongue root in its natural 
neutral position, we label those vowels are Unadvanced Tongue Root i.e. (-ATR) 
vowels. Some examples of (+ATR) vowels are: /i, e, u, o/, and examples of (-ATR) 
vowels are /ɪ, ɛ, ɔ/.

Having discussed the nature of vowel sounds and the parametres used in 
describing the vowel sounds of your language, we now focus our attention on 
the production of consonants.
The concept of consonant
As was mentioned earlier in the section, consonant is another type of speech sounds 
apart from vowel. The concept consonant refers to a speech sound in which during 
production the breath, which we have termed airflow, is at least obstructed. Based 
on this explanation, we can contrast vowel and consonant by saying that while in 
the production of vowel there is very minimal or no obstruction of airflow, there 
is significant obstruction of airflow when producing consonants. We combined 
vowels and consonants form a word.
Description of consonants
When we want to describe a consonant, there are parametres that are used for 
that purpose. The three parametres used to describe consonants are: place of 
articulation manner of articulation, and voicing. We will discuss each of the three 
parametres and provide examples to illustrate it. Anye baa sa nɛ anye a delge 
nnɔtɔwor so, ekpaana nɛ anyee bɛso wɔtɔ nna. Ekpa ntuŋ sa mo so nɛ anyee bɔlɔ 
a delge nnɔtɔwor so ela: kakpa nɛ bu kɔ a tere amo, afuu be keyigeto nɛ ebol. 
Anyeeŋ buwito ekpaana na n shin sa amobe akeniso.

Place of articulation:
This refers to a point of contact between two organs of speech during production 
of consonant sounds. As was observed in the video on speech sounds, some of the 
places of articulation in a Ghanaian language are bilabial, labio-dental, alveolar, 
palatal, velar, etc. The following are some places of articulation and the consonants 
of a Ghanaian language that are produced in these places. Kakpa nɛ bu kɔ a tere: 
Kede ela mboŋ anyɔ monɛ amalgasɔ anyɔ na bee bir abarso ashuŋ nnɔtɔwor be 
ketere to. Fanɛ anye ka peshe ashi vidiyo na be kamalga na to na, mboŋana monɛ 
anye kɔ a tii nnɔtɔwor Ngbanyato be ako ela: nnɔpirbi, nnɔpirbi nɛ anyi, anyifar, 
kɔnɔbuŋmantaŋ nɛ adamta. Mboŋ nɛ anye kɔ a tii amo nɛ Ngbanya be nnɔtɔwor 
monɛ a bee tii be ako nde.
• Bilabial: In producing bilabial sounds, we bring our two lips closely together. 
For example, /p, b, m/. nnɔpirbi: fo baa sha ketii nnɔpirbi be kelɔntorwor, 
anyee bra nnɔpirbi anyɔ na abarso nna. Fanɛ /p, b, m/
• Alveolar: When producing an alveolar sound, we bring our front part of the 
tongue to the hard palate. Some examples of alveolar sounds are /t, d, s, n/ 
Anyifar: Fo baa sha ketii anyifar be kelɔntorwor, anyee ta kudundunloŋ be 
kɔnɔso nna m ba bir anyifar so. Anyifar be alɔntorwor be akeniso ko nde: /t, 
d, s, n/
• Labio-dental:Labio-dental sounds are produced by touching your upper set 
of the teeth with your lower lip. For example, /f/. Nnɔpirbi nɛ anyi: Fo baa 
sha ketii nnɔpirbi nɛ anyi be kelɔntorwor, fobe esoso be anyi na bee bir fobe 
kaseto be kɔnɔpirbi na so nna.
• Palatal: In producing palatal sounds, we raise the centre of our tongue towards 
the hard palate. An example of palatal sound is /j/. Kɔnɔbuŋmantaŋ: Fo 
baa sha ketii Kɔnɔbuŋmantaŋ be kelɔntorwor, fee ta fobe kudundunloŋ be 
mfrinto na nna m bir fobe anyifar na so. /j/
• Velar: When producing velar sounds, we push the back of our tongue towards 
the velum or the soft palate. Some examples of velar sounds are /k, g/. 
Kɔnɔbuŋmantaŋkarase: Fo baa tii Kɔnɔbuŋmantaŋkarase be kelɔntorwor, 
fee ŋin fobe kudundunloŋ be kaman nna a yɔ fobe kɔnɔbuŋmantaŋkarase 
be kabaso.

Manner of articulation:
This refers to how the airflow is obstructed in the course of production of 
consonant sounds. There are degrees of obstruction of airflow during speech 
sounds production. For example, in some consonants, in their production there 
is a momentary complete blocking or obstruction and sudden release of airflow. 
Based on the degree of closure or obstruction, some manners of articulation can 
be identified with consonants of a Ghanaian language. the articulators configure 
and interact during the production of speech sound. Some examples of manners 
of articulation of consonants include stops, fricatives, affricate, nasal, lateral, 
etc. The following are some manners of articulation and examples of consonant 
sounds of a Ghanaian language produced in those manners.
Afuu be keyigeto: Kede bee ŋini kananɛ anyee yige afuu to nna ashi alɔntorwor 
be ketere to. Afuu be keyigeto ashi nnɔtowor be tii to kɔ ekpa damta nna. Fanɛ 
nnɔtɔwor ko be ketii to, fee kuŋ afuu na kikɛ nna pɔɛ n shi ŋ shinɛ a lar. Nkpal 
amobe afuu be keyigeto to be ekpaana ka shi so Ngbanyato kɔ loŋ be nnɔtɔwor be 
ntuŋso nna. Amalgasɔ na e naa bir abarso saŋɛ nɛ anye baa tii nnɔtɔwor. Afuu be 
keyigeto be akeniso ko ela akuŋso, afɛrgeso tenteŋ, afɛrgeso shimbi, lermmunato 
nɛ adamta.
• Stops: As the name suggests, in producing stop sounds, the continuous 
airflow is completely stopped or obstructed momentarily or briefly. The 
obstructed airflow is released suddenly. For example, /p, b, t, d, k, g, m, n/. 
Based on where the trapped or obstructed airflow is released from, we can 
categorize stop sounds into two, namely oral stop and nasal stop. When the 
trapped air is released through the mouth, it is known as plosive, e.g. /p, b, 
t, d, k, g/. On the other hand, when the trapped air is released through the 
nose, it is known as nasal stop, e.g. /m, n/. Akuŋso: Fanɛ kananɛ kumobe 
ketere na bee ŋini na, afuu na be eshile na bee kuŋ/yili nna epolto n shin 
ba lar nɛ eleŋso. Fanɛ /p, b, t, d, k, g, m, n/. Nɛ fo bɛso kakpa nɛ afuu na 
be keyigeto na bee shi na, anyeeŋ tiŋ ta amo n wɔtɔ ntuŋ nyɔ so, kɔnɔto be 
akuŋso nɛ kamunato be akuŋso. Nɛ afuu kuŋso na baŋ ba lar kɔnɔ to, kumo 
ela apanteso, fanɛ /p, b, d, t, k, g/. Ama nɛ afuu kuŋso na baŋ ba lar kamuna 
to, kumo ela akuŋso larmmunato fanɛ /m, n/.
• Fricative: For the production of fricative, there is no complete obstruction 
of airflow but rather a narrow space so that airflow passes through the space 
gradually thereby causing friction. Some examples of fricative sounds are /f, 
s/. Afirgeso tenteŋ: Ama afirgeso shimbi be ketii to afuu na kikɛ maa kuŋ, 
a bee yige kaboŋ gbre nna nɛ afuu na e ba firgeso a lar. Kumobe akeniso ko 
nde, /f, s/

• Affricate: In producing affricate sounds, there are two stages involved; 
first there is a complete obstruction of airflow, and in the final stages the 
obstructed airflow is released gradually (not suddenly). Some examples 
include /tʃ/ as applicable in a Ghanaian language. Afirgeso shimbi: Fo baa 
tii afirgeso tenteŋ be kelɔntorwor, ekpa ntuŋ nyɔ e wɔtɔ; sososo afuu na bee 
kuŋ nna cheche, nɛ lalaluwe nɛ afuu na e ba lar gbre gbre. Amobe akeniso 
ko ela /tʃ/.
• Lateral: In the production of lateral sound, the front part of the tongue 
will touch the alveolar ridge allowing airflow from only the side of the 
mouth. An example of a lateral sound is /l/. Kudundunloŋkar: Fo baa tii 
Kudundunloŋkar be kelɔntorwor, fobe kudundunloŋ na be ekarso bee bata 
fobe Kɔnɔbuŋmantaŋ nna a sa nɛ afuu bee bulɔ fobe kɔnɔ be kaba a lar. 
Kumobe kekeniso ela /l/.
• Trill: Trill sound is produced by the tongue, which is the active articulator, 
touching the passive articulator; the alveolar ridge in quick succession. An 
example of a trill sound is /r/. Chaamaŋto: Kudundunloŋ ela kemalgasɔ 
monɛ ku bee tii chaamaŋto, kumo ela kamalgasɔ gboŋ monɛ ku bee cha 
fobe kɔnɔto a bata anyifarkarase na manaŋmanaŋ
Voicing:
My dear learner, the third parametre we use in describing consonant sounds is the 
voicing. When we are making or producing consonant sounds, our vocal folds, 
which are inside our glottis assumes two states; either it is vibrating or it is not 
vibrating. When the vocal folds are vibrating, the sounds we produce are known 
as voiced consonants. On the other hand, when the vocal folds are not vibrating 
when articulating consonant sounds we call those consonant sounds voiceless 
sounds. Some examples of voiced consonants include /g/, /d/, /m/, /b/, and 
voiceless consonants include /f/, /s/, /k/, /t/, / ʃ/, etc. Ma bebiipo lɛla, ekpa sasepo 
monɛ anye naa kɔ a tii nnɔtowor ela ebol. Anye baa tii nnɔtoworana, anyebe lɔntor 
to be eblaŋ nɛ a wɔ anyebe lɔntorpe na bee wɔrɔ asheŋ anyɔ nna: a bee chichato 
nna nko a maa chichato. Lɔntorpe na baa chichato, nnɔtowor monɛ anyee tii na 
la amonɛ a kɔ ebol nna. Ama nɛ anye baa tii nnɔtowor nɛ lɔntorpe na baa maa 
chichato, anyee tere loŋ peya na nnɔtowor monɛ a paŋ ebol nna. Nnɔtowor monɛ 
a kɔ ebol be ako ela: /g/, /d/, /m/, /b/, nɛ amonɛ a paŋ ebol na malɛ be ako la: /f/, 
/s/, /k/, /t/, / ʃ/, nɛ adamta.

SOUND DISTRIBUTION
The concept sound distribution simply refers to the position in a word where 
speech sounds can occur in a language. Every language has some restrictions on 
where it can permit a speech sound to occur. The three positions that speech sounds 
can occur in word are initial position, medial position, or final positions. Let us 
begin our discussions with the distribution of vowels.Alɔntorwor be kechigeto 
kikɛ e baa la kamalgaba be kaboŋ nɛ kelɔntorwor na beeŋ tiŋ a wɔ ashi ngbar na 
to. Ngbar kikɛ kɔ kamalgaba be kaboŋ nɛ alɔntorwor ko beeŋ tiŋ a wɔ nɛ kaboŋ 
nɛ a maaŋ tiŋ a wɔ nna. Mboŋ asa monɛ alɔntorwor bee tiŋ a wɔ ashi kamalgaba 
to ela kɔranishito, kɔrnfrinto nɛ kɔrmmanto. Anyee fara anyebe kasɔbii na nɛ 
eboltowor be nchigeto.
Vowel Distribution Eboltowor be kechigeto
Vowel distribution simply refers to the position that a vowel can occur in a word 
in a Ghanaian language. When a vowel occurs at the beginning of a word, we 
say it has occurred in a word initial position. When it occurs at the middle of a 
word, we refer to that position as the word medial position, while when it occurs 
at the end of a word, it is referred to as word final position. From the explanation 
above, it is clear that languages treat vowel distributions differently. It is also 
important to note that some of the vowels can occur in all the three positions in 
words in a language. Let us consider in the example below the distribution of the 
vowel /a/ in the words: NB: Please, replace examples with appropriate ones in a

INTRODUCTION
This section discusses identification of key ideas in texts and discourse. It 
always gives information on specific ideas or knowledge to the reader or hearer. 
The information given may come from all perspectives such as education, 
industrialisation, mining among others. It may also indicate some cultural values 
such as respect, tolerance and patience. Identifying key ideas gives you a better 
understanding of the discourse. It also enhances your critical thinking skills and 
interpretation abilities. There are types of reading techniques namely skimming 
and scanning and the application of any of the type enables you to get the right 
information demanded at any time. Knowledge of the types is therefore essential 
in our everyday life. The concept of oral interpretation will also be discussed. We 
shall discuss the skills needed for effective interpretation. Interpretation plays 
important roles in facilitating communication across language barriers.
At the end of this section, you should be able to
• Identify key ideas from appropriate discourse. E.g., cultural values 
(respect, kindness, tolerance and others), education, child trafficking, 
environment, industrialisation in Ghana, mining, GESI etc.,
• Discuss ideas and relevant opinions from selected discourse. E.g., 
cultural values (respect, kindness, tolerance and others), education, 
child trafficking, environment, industrialisation in Ghana, mining, GESI, 
STEM, etc.
Key Ideas
• Key ideas are the main messages that is relevant in any discourse. Some 
of the key ideas may center on cultural values such as respect, kindness, 
tolerance, patience, etc. In any discourse you can share relevant opinions

on any discourse appropriately and interpret any discourse in your own

• Dear learner, before leaving home for your present school, what are the 
main points from the conversation you had with your parent/guardian? 
Share with peers.
• The main points you shared with your peers are known to as key ideas. 
Key ideas are the essential ideas that the author or speaker wants to give 
to the reader or hearer/listener respectively. The ideas may include the 
claims, the reasons, conclusions, definitions, classifications, comparisons, 
evaluations, recommendations, etc. Key ideas can be expressed explicitly 
or implicitly.
• For you to identify the key ideas in discourse there is the need for you 
to understand the main concepts, arguments, and the points made. Note 
that the discourse could deal with any topic such as mining, teenage 
pregnancy, natural disaster, educational issues among others. It must also 
be pointed out that it could also come in a text form, video or picture or 
all the forms mentioned.
• In summary, my dear learner to identify the key ideas in a discourse which 
may be written or oral or visual, you may need to answer the following 
questions
1. Find who or what the passage discusses: Does this passage discuss a 
person, group of people or an entity?
2. Ask when the event took place: Does the information contain a reference 
to time?
3. Find where the event took place: Does the text name a place?
4. Ask why the event took place: Do you find a reason or explanation for 
something that happened?
5. Ask how the event took place: Does this information indicate a method 
or a theory?

WHAT IS DISCOURSE

Key ideas
 Skimming is going through a text rapidly to get the general information 
in the text while scanning involves looking for a specific information in 
a text. Scanning is a process of reading in which your eyes quickly run 
through a piece of text to find a piece of relevant information. Scanning 
and skimming are two different concepts of reading.
TYPES OF READING
There are types of reading skill or technique namely skimming, scanning, 
intensive reading and extensive reading. Dear learner, in this lesson you shall 
learn skimming and scanning techniques of reading.
Skimming
Skimming is a reading technique used to quickly identify the main ideas or key 
points in a text. It is the action of reading something quickly so as to note only the 
important points. Basically, skimming is reading rapidly in order to get a general 
overview of the material read. It is used to find specific facts in texts. It involves 
glancing over the material, focusing on headings, subheadings, bold text and key 
phrases to get a general understanding of the content. Skimming is useful when; 
time is limited, looking for specific information, you want to get an overview 
8
SECTION2 SHARING IDEAS AND ORAL INTERPRETATION
before reading in-depth and you are dealing with a large amount of text. Below 
are the skimming types.
Preview: An opportunity to view something before it is acquired or becomes 
generally available. Preview is done in an effort to learn about the ideas presented 
and the structure of their development.
Overview: Used to sample the reading material more thoroughly. A general review 
or summary of a subject.
Review: The review is done to re-familiarise yourself with the material you have 
previously read thoroughly or skimmed. A formal assessment of something with 
the intention of instituting a change if necessary.
Learner, in skimming, you can follow these steps
1. Read the title
2. Read the headings and sub-headings as well as topic sentences in each 
paragraph
3. Look for important information such as date, names and unusual words.
4. Read the conclusion

In summary you have learnt skimming and the steps as well as the types of 
skimming which you can apply. Dear learner, let us examine what is scanning.
Scanning
Scanning is reading rapidly in order to find facts without reading everything. 
Scanning helps you locate a particular fact while skimming tells you what general 
information is within a section.
Scanning involves looking for a specific information in a text. It can also be said 
to be a process of reading in which your eyes quickly run through a piece of text 
to find a piece of relevant information. In scanning the reader looks for a piece 
of specific information. An example of scanning is searching for the meaning 
of a word in a dictionary. Scanning helps the reader to locate particular facts in 
an entire text quickly. Students often use scanning when solving their reading 
comprehension questions.
It is important to know the purpose for scanning. You should know what you are 
searching for, eg title of a book, a website, a reference material, a particular word 
or phrase and a particular story you want to read etc. You should know how the 
material is structures either alphabetically, non-alphabetically, chronologically, 
by category, by titles /headings, by textual sense, by numbers among others.
Scanning helps a learner to read more and to develop love for reading.
When to scan
1. Scan before reading
2. Scan a number of questions to identify the one which you are most 
comfortable answering
3. When searching for particular information such as date, keywords etc.
The following shows how to do scanning after getting overview of a text and 
identifying the sections of the text you want to read.
1. Start scanning the text by moving your eyes and fingers quickly over it
2. When you have identified the information, word or the phrase you are 
searching for, read the information surrounding the word carefully
3. When you identified the information that requires attention, you read it 
thoroughly slowly.

Oral Interpretation and translation
At the end of the sub-strand you should be able to:
 Discuss oral interpretation focusing on effective listening, encoding and 
decoding,
Key Ideas
 Oral interpretation is reframing the meaning of a speech most often orally 
into another language. The original language is the source language 
and the language in which it is rendered is the target language. In oral 
interpretation you must note the cultural differences and be accurate in 
giving the meaning of what you are to render in the language orally.
CONTENT
Interpretation is listening to a message in one language and rendering it orally 
in another language maintaining the original meaning, tone and context. It 
is the stylistic representation of a creative work or dramatic role. It is the act 
of explaining, reframing, or otherwise showing your own understanding of 
something. In interpretation you first have to understand the text or the piece 
given to you and then explain in your own words. In broader terms it is rendering 
a spoken or signed message into another spoken or signed language preserving 
the register and meaning of the source language content.
Dear learner, it must be noted that before you can do any interpretation, you must 
be well versed in the source and target language. Interpretation can be performed 
either simultaneously or consecutively between users of different languages.
Dear learner, know that in interpreting you do not embellish or over-exaggerate. 
State the ideas clearly. In interpreting you need to listen carefully, decode and 
encode as they serve as the process of communication and interpreting.

What is Encoding Manɛ ela kebɔaya be 
kenuto?
Encoding is the process of translating information into a form that can be 
transmitted to another person or system. It involves interpreting and understanding 
a text or message. It involves reading or receiving the text, recognize the words, 
phrases and sentences, interpret the meaning, context and intent behind the text 
and understand the cultural, linguistic and semantic nuances. 
Kebɔaya be kenuto: Kebɔaya be kenuto ela ekpa nɛ fee bulɔso a kilgi kebɔaya a 
yɔ kananɛ ku beeŋ tiŋ tu esa pɔtɛ. Kumo e baa la kebɔaya be kepinto nɛ kebɔaya 
pɔlso be kefiito be kebuwito. Ku kɔ kebɔaya na be kekraŋ nko kesɔ, mmalgaba, 
mmalgafolshiŋ nɛ mmalgafol na be kepin, kefiito na be kebuwito, apuntosɔ nɛ 
mfɛra monɛ ku wɔ kebɔaya na be kesibɛ be kaman n shin pin edaŋkaresheŋ na be 
mbarga to.
Decoding Kebɔaya be kekute
This is the process of creating a text or message. It involves the interpretation 
and translation of coded information into a comprehensible form. This is how an 
audience is able to understand and interpret the message. Decoding can also be 
explained as transforming ideas, thoughts, or messages into spoken text. 
Kebɔaya be kekute: Kede ela ekpa monɛ fee bulɔso a kuu kebɔaya nko kasibɛ. Ku 
la ekpa monɛ fee bulɔ a buwito nko a kilgi kebɔaya muluŋ to nna a yɔ kananɛ ku 
beeŋ tiŋ pinto. Loŋ nɛ benupo bee tiŋ a pin kebɔaya na to a buwi kumobe kefiito. 
Anyeeŋ naŋ tiŋ ŋinito fanɛ kebɔaya be kekute ela alakal, afɛso nko abɔaya be 
kekilgi n yɔ kamalga to.
You need to know the following to do oral interpretation
1. Listen attentively.
2. You should be fluent in both languages.
3. Keep to the meaning of the test or speech in the original language.
4. Keep pace with the dialogue.

Meeŋ bargato ntuŋ wurbi to n shin sibɛ asɔ kudu monɛ a wɔ ebiikpabuu to 
nko n chambɔ kumo. Menye e ta mmalgaba anyɔ n tiiso ta n laŋɛ kananɛ 
ebiikpa be epunto nɛ kowu bee wɔrɔ fo. Menyebe katuŋ nɛ ntuŋ pɔtɛana kɔ 
lakal koŋwule aa?
MANƐ ELA ATERE?
Ketere ela kananɛ ba tere bomin, kaboŋ, kusɔbɔaya, nko kusɔ. Atere ko gba bee 
ka la alakal, nko kebawɔtɔ ko nna.
Atere be ntuŋso
Atere kpra
Atere kpra ela atere monɛ bu kɔ a tere baasa, kaboŋ nko kusɔ nɛ ku la Ebɔrɛ be 
kusɔtooso nko bomin be kusɔ lɔŋɛ so. Atere kpra kikɛ bee fara nɛ kelɔntorwor 
gboŋ nna kamalgafol be kaboŋ kama nɛ ku wɔ. Amobe akeniso ko nde:
Baasa be atere: Amaabaŋɛ, Ntareka, Awundre, Dari, Kanyiti, Nyɛfiyanɔto, Ledi, 
nɛ adamta.
Mboŋ be atere: Busunu, Daboya, Bɔnyaŋ, Sɔr, Afadjato, nɛ adamta.
Nchɛ nɛ a wɔ bɔkwɛ to: Aledi, Ataniya, Atalata, Alariba, nɛ amo nɛ a ka.
Kafɛ to be afol : Jintigi, Damba be kayɛrbi, Damba, Kafɔrawajɛ, Kajululu, nɛ 
amo nɛ a ka.
Mboŋ ko : Komfo Anokye be Ashibiti gboŋ, Jubilee be Lambuu, Ghana be 
Yunivasiti, nɛ adamta.
Nchu be atere: Bɔnyaŋ, Volta, Sɔr, Pra, Mole, nɛ adamta.
Atere jewulebi
Ade la asɔ be atere nna (dimedi, kusɔ, kaboŋ, ketere nko mfɛra ko), nɛ a maŋ la 
atere kpra (keni esoso ndoŋ). A maa fara nɛ kelɔntorwor gboŋ ama a baa junkpar 
kamalgafol nna. Amo nɛ atanyusobi nɛ adulwiso pɔtɛ bee tiŋ a wiɛ abarto nna. 
Akeniso ko ela klembi, buku, laŋ, kɔrɔtɔ, lɔr, ebiikpabuu, egbalsibɛso, nchu, nɛ 
adamta.

Atere yoyul
Ade la mmalgaba nna nɛ a bee yili a sa asɔ monɛ anye maaŋ tiŋ wu kinishi so ama 
a kɔ atere kachina to. Ade bee yili a sa alakal monɛ anye maa wu, a nu amobe 
efɛ nko a bata amo. A bee delge adabi, alakal nɛ kananɛ mfɛra bee wɔrɔ fo so 
nna. Akeniso ko ela kagbenefuli, kasha, kagbenejajɛ, kashinteŋ, kanyiesheŋ nɛ 
adamta.
Atere nyifu
Ade la asɔ gbagba monɛ anyeeŋ tiŋ wu n shin tiŋ bata nna. Awɔ durnyaŋ to nna 
nɛ anyeeŋ tiŋ wu amo gbagba to. A bee yili nna a sa kusɔ ko nko esa ko nɛ anyeeŋ 
tiŋ ta anyebe alakal anu na (kebata, kenu, kewu, kedufɛ nɛ keda n keni) m pin. 
Atere nyifu be akeniso ko ela kejembu, tebul, nchu, shishɛr, kakure, jebote, kabɛ, 
nɛ adamta.

Tise atere ere to n wɔtɔ ntuŋ so fanɛ atere kpra, atere jewulebi, atere yoyul, nɛ 
atere nyifu. Ŋini kusɔ mo so nɛ fo wɔtɔ amo katuŋ kama na to.
i. eŋinipo
ii. tebul

iv. Ntareka

vi. kagbenefuli
vii. kɔnɔkoŋwule
viii. kabɛ
ix. afuu
x. kejembu

ii. Menye e ta atere monɛ menye pin kebɔaya na to na n wɔtɔ atere be ntuŋ ana na to.

Kumu: Kechambɔ Ma Kade be Kibɛ To
Ashi ma kadeto, kaboŋ wiliwili ko wɔtɔ nɛ ba tere kumo kibɛto. Ku la kaboŋ 
be mfrinto nna nɛ baasa bee chala a fa n kaa tɔ asɔ be yiri kikɛ. Ashi asɔrso 
lɛla nɛ epofantaŋ to n yɔ asɔbuuso, asɔpelso, nɛ lanto be asɔana gba, feeŋ tiŋ 
wu fanɛ kusɔ kama ndoŋ.
Bɔkwɛ be lalaluwe kikɛ ma nɛ mabe kanaŋ bee yɔ kibɛ na to nna n ya ka tɔ 
anyebe asɔ. Anye ka bee fo, mee nu asɔfapoana ka bee ponte aworso a tii 
bumobe asɔ be ayawu nɛ afɛdewurana ka bee jɔto eleŋso a kulti be awor.
Kusɔ nɛ n daŋ kuwu sososo ela asɔrso nɛ epɔfantaŋ lɛla monɛ bu nase yɛrr 
nɛnɛ ashi apata na to. Alemu lɛla, akodu kachunɔnyifu belso, nɛ agɔndɔ 
kefitiribumbuŋ nyikpɛso kikɛ wɔtɔ. Ajibi bumbuŋ be efɛ sɔ afuu na kikɛ nɛ ku 
bee wɔrɔ ma fanɛ n lara ma asɔ shaso damta.
Kumo nɛ ku bɛso, anye bulɔ afɛde nɛ a bee fa asɔbuuso nɛ asɔwurbi na be 
kaboŋ na. Nle nyikpɛso, atoto be abatoro, nɛ ashembi nyikpɛso pɛ ma lakal. 
Mee sha kebaa keni kananɛ bu ta amo m bɛ na to a fin kusɔbuuso monɛ ku 
daga nɛ n tii mabe asɔ so.
Anye ka kraa nite kibɛ na to nɛ anye ba afɛde monɛ a bee fa asɔpɛlso nɛ 
akonde. Ashi abinfure lɛlaana nɛ asɔ fiilito to n yɔ abebi to, kebia kama be 
edare to be kusɔpelso wɔ ndoŋ. Maŋ tiŋ kuŋ mabe kumu nɛ emushe ngbuŋto 
nkpal n ka wu kagbenefuli monɛ ku wɔ mbia pɔtɛ be anishiana to bu ka bee 
keni asɔpelso nɛ bu ta n nase na.
Lalaluwe, anye fo kibɛ to be kaboŋ monɛ ba fa lanto be asɔ na. Mfa, anye wu 
lanto be kusɔkama ashi edaŋɛkpa nɛ farfarbi be asɔ to n yɔ kaboŋ be kemiɛto 
be asɔ to. Nnio bee wushi eyur nna n lara kusɔkama monɛ anye bee sha nɛ 
malɛ bee chɛto a sulɔ alɔkɔ na.
Anyeeŋ ta n chɛso n mige atere be ntuŋ damta to n tiiso
Adamtato tere / Ntuŋso tere
A la atere monɛ a bee yili nna a sa katuŋ. Katuŋ na beeŋ tiŋ a la asɔ be katuŋ, 
asɔbɔaya peya nko baasa be katuŋ. Akeniso ko ela dimedi, nshɛboŋpo, ngbar, 
abuku, mbuibi, nɛ adamta. Amo nɛ amo, a bee yili a sa asɔ, asɔbɔaya nko baasa 
damta ama a la kukoŋwule nna.

SECTION 3 MMALGABA NƐ NGBAR BE KAPƆR
Manɛ ela kedulwiso?
Ntuŋso to, menye e sa mmalgaba asa monɛ menyeeŋ ta n delge asɔ/baasa ere so;
- Fobe ebiikpabuu
- Fo teri kpakpaso
- Fobe tebul
- Kananɛ fobe sukuru to du
Kedulwiso ela kamalgaba monɛ bu kɔ a delge nko a buwi ketere so nɛnɛ. Adulwiso 
la mmalgaba nna nɛ bu kɔ amo a sa abɔaya ta n laŋɛ kananɛ esa nko kusɔ du 
be kabaso. Adulwiso be akeniso ko ela kefitiribumbuŋ, kenyɔso, kachunɔnyifu, 
kufuful, shimbi, tenteŋ, kebita, gboŋ, gboŋgboŋi, fimbi, dendlembi, kagbenefuli, 
kagbenejajɛ, kanyiasheŋ, kashinteŋ, nɛ adamta. Kananɛ adulwiso ere be ako bee 
luri mmalgafol to nde.
i. Mee sha alaŋ dra.
ii. Kebianyɛnsobi na du tenteŋ n shin wɔlso.
iii. Amaabaŋɛ du wɔrɛwɔrɛbi achɔ mo siponyɛn.
Ashi (i) to, “dra” bee delgeso nko a buwito alaŋ be dubi monɛ emalgapo na bee 
sha nna. Ashi (ii) to, “tenteŋ” nɛ “wɔlso” bee delge kebianyɛnsobi na be kapɔr 
so nna. Ashi (iii) to, bu ta “wɔrɛwɔrɛbi” na nna n ta Amaabaŋɛ nɛ mo siponyɛn 
be kanyiasheŋ a kesar abar.
Adulwiso be ntuŋso
Adulwiso kɔ ntuŋso nɛ a kɔr abarto, amobe atenini nɛ feeŋ bii ela;
-  Kananɛ kusɔ sa be adulwiso
-  Kesatobi be adulwiso
-  Adelgesobi be adulwiso
Kananɛ kusɔ sa be adulwiso
Kede bee shuŋ fanɛ kananɛ kusɔ sa be ntilemu nna (kede, kumo, ade, amo) a shuŋ 
fanɛ adelgeso a ŋini kusɔ monɛ ku bee delgeso na nko a buwi ketere be kananɛ ku 
du to nɛnɛ. Keni ade kaseto ere.
a.  Ekuloŋ na la kepupɔr nna.
b. Kache na e wɔ alaŋ naa.
c. Kowu na la ma tuto peya nna.
c. Shamoya e na tɔ alaŋ ana ere.
10

Ketankesar be adulwiso
Bu kɔ amo nna a ta baasa nko asɔ pɔtɛana a kesar abar. Ketankesar abar be 
adulwiso ere be ako ela fimbi achɔ, jenjreŋ achɔ, shibi achɔ, wɔrɛwɔrɛbi achɔ, nɛ 
adamta. Anye ta ketankesar be adulwiso ere be ako n shuŋ kaseto ere na.
a. Ade la ajibi putɔputɔ nna.
b. Ntareka du wɔrɛwɔrɛbi achɔ Dari.
c. Ekuloŋ fuful na du manaŋmanaŋ achɔ kenyɔso na.
d. Fo amanshɛrbi du fimbi achɔ meya.
Kesatobi be adulwiso
Adelgeso ere bee sa abɔaya nna ta n laŋɛ kananɛ asɔ sa be kabaso. Asatobi bee 
shuŋ adelgeso be kushuŋ nna nkpalmanɛso, a bee buwi ketere na to nna a kaŋɛ 
anye kananɛ ku sa. Keni akeniso ere.
a. N tɔ amalo gberɛ.
b. E daŋɛ afule anyɔ
c. E bee sha shikari gberɛbi.
d. Abuku damta wɔ mabe daka to.
Adelgesobi be adulwiso
Adelgesobi be adulwiso ela adulwiso monɛ a bee delge ketere be adabi so nko a 
buwi ketere be kananɛ ku du to nɛnɛ. A la adulwiso monɛ a bee delge atere nna. 
Adulwiso be akeniso damta wɔ katuŋ ere to nna. Keni ade kaseto ere.
a. Ekuloŋ na la kedra nna.
b. N kɔ buku fimbi.
c. Ajibi na kɔ kayɛlga.
d. N wu ekuloŋ gboŋ.
Kushuŋ
1.  Laŋɛ n ya keni mmalgaba monɛ fo pin kasɔbii ere be sososo na. Ta amo 
n wɔtɔ ntuŋso to fanɛ ketankesar be adulwiso, asatobi be adulwiso nko 
adelgesobi be adulwiso. Sibɛ katuŋ kama be akeniso n tiiso.
2.  Kraŋ kaseto be kebɔaya ere n shin pin adulwiso monɛ a wɔ kumo to. Ta 
adulwiso monɛ fo pin na n wɔtɔ ntuŋso fanɛ ketankesar be adulwiso,

asatobi be adulwiso nko adelgesobi be adulwiso n shin wɔrɔ shiriya nɛ 
fo ta fobe atuwebi n sa bebiipo kikɛ.
Koshinyɛn ka baŋ boŋ kelusasepo nɛ Kemolwɔpe ebi kikɛ mol nɛ bu tu bumobe 
ewura. Bewurabi na daŋ buu asɔ fuful nna. Bu daŋ ta achebi fuful nna n chɛ 
bumobe amu n saa nite nɛ aya fuloŋ.
Bu daŋ chala nna nɛ bu bunya ewura na. Ku la daŋkare na fanɛ ewura ere 
mo nananyɛn e daŋ molwɔ kade ere ebi nɛ akoŋ be kapliɛ so beeŋ wɔrɔ nfɛ 
kanaŋ ko. E daŋ molwɔ bumo na saŋɛ monɛ edɛ daŋ chɔ kadeebi be ndɔana 
kikɛ kapaso ko nɛ akoŋ daa fuwe kadeebi kikɛ a yɔ na. Akoŋ daŋ chɔrɔ alaŋ 
kikɛ n sa nɛ bu bɛle n lara tama kikɛ.
Enananyɛn ere e daŋ ta mobe adɔjibi damta ashi kadebi n molwɔ baasa na. 
Baasa na ta kanyɛn na n kii bumobe ewura aŋini bumobe kagbenefuli nɛ 
mobe kakɛ na. Kafɛ kikɛ baa bunya mo nna a ŋini mobe adabi lela na so.
Fanɛ kaseto be akeniso ere to na, ketere beeŋ tiŋ junkpar adelgesobi be adulwiso 
na nɛ a maŋ bɛ abarso.
a.  Laŋ na walɛ.
b. Keshembi monɛ fo wɔtɔ na bee nyikpɛ
c. Amangu nɛ fee ji na wɔbel.
d. Kedibi monɛ n wu na wɔnteŋ.
Adelgesobi be adulwiso ere nɛ atere monɛ a bee delge so na beeŋ tiŋ bɛ abarso. 
Ngbanyato, ketere na bee junkpar nna nɛ kedulwiso na malɛ e bɛ kumo so. Keni 
ade kaseto ere:
a. Laŋ lɛla nde.
b. N wu kedibi tenteŋ.
c. N nio tɔ kebɔtoshembi nyikpɛso n sa ma.
d. Mee ji amangu belbelso karɛchɛ kama.

1.  Menye e ta adulwiso ere n wɔtɔ amobe ntuŋso to n shin ta menyebe 
atuwebi n ŋini. Ntuŋana e ŋini kusɔ mo so nɛ bu ta amo n wɔtɔ loŋ be 
adulwiso be ntuŋ na to.

ii.   nteŋ

iv.  kayɛlga
v.  bargato
vi.  kepeper
vii.  kelubi
viii.  kebɔrɛwɔlpa
ix.  nyaŋnyaŋ
x.  fimbi
xi.  putɔputɔ
xii.  asa
xiii.  gberɛ
2.  Kraŋ kebɔaya ere nɛnɛ n shin tuwe mbishi monɛ a bɛso ere.
i.  Tiseto adulwiso monɛ a wɔ kebɔaya na to kikɛ.
ii.  Ta adulwiso monɛ fo pin na kikɛ n wɔtɔ amobe ntuŋso to.
iii.  Ta adulwiso be katuŋ kama nɛ fo pin na be akeniso anu nu n kuu mmalgafol.
Jebuni nite mobe sososo n yɔ nɛ e ya chɔrɔ mo daa kadegboŋto. E ka baŋ gbelge 
ekuloŋ to, ku wɔrɔ mo mamachi nɛ kadegboŋto be kebawɔtɔ. e fara a keni ebu 
tenteŋ ana, aborbi lela, nɛ kananɛ baasa bee nite akulti. Kesheŋ keni sa nɛ Jebuni 
teŋso ketere mo daa nɛ e baa ta mo ekuloŋ be eyilikpa na. E ka baŋ nyiŋi epulto 
nɛ e lara mobe tangrafo dra mobe lɔkɔ lembir to n fara a tare mo daa. Pɔɛ nɛ 
tangrafo na e kuuto, ekuloŋ fuful ko barga gbre m yili m mata kaboŋ mo nɛ e yili 
na. E bee mushe m buwi anishito be kukuloŋ na n luri n china to. Nkpal mo daa 
be laŋto nɛ kakpa monɛ e yili na ka la a miniti kuduanu so, ku maŋ char nɛ bu 
fo laŋto. E ka wushi nɛnɛ n luwe, nɛ bu sa mo ajibi belbelso nɛ e ji n tuwe akoŋ.

MANƐ ELA KUSHUŊSO?
Manɛ nɛ fo wɔrɔ kachepur ere? Tiseto amo to n nase.
Manɛ nɛ fee fɛ ta n laŋɛ fobe sukuru pɔtɛ be kasɔbii be kumu be kabaso? Tiseto 
fobe mfɛra to.
Wɔrɔ aniya m buwito fobe lakal to n ŋini fo baraana ebiikpa.
Kushuŋso ela kamalgaba monɛ bu kɔ a ŋini kesheŋwɔrɔ.  Kushuŋso naa la 
kamalgaba nko kamalgafolshiŋ nna a ŋini kananɛ kesheŋ bee wɔrɔ. (akeniso fanɛ

Ngbanyato be kasibɛ be mbra
KASOTOFUTI
Kaba ere bee mige mbra monɛ baa bɛso a sibɛ Ngbanyato nna. Anyeeŋ bir kasibɛ 
be mbra be kelijima ta n laŋɛ atere, ashuŋso, ntilemu nɛ adulwiso be kabaso. 
Sososo, anyeeŋ bir mbra nɛ a bee kuŋ atere be kelijima, m ba ta ntilemu, adulwiso, 
ashuŋso nɛ adelgeso m ba bɛso. Kede la kebla fo ase nɛnɛ nna ta n laŋɛ Ngbanyato 
be atere, ntilemu, adulwiso, ashuŋso nɛ adelgeso be mbra nɛ keta n shuŋ be kabaso 
nna. Mbra nɛ fo bii Ngbanyato na nɛ asɔ pɔtɛ nɛ fee bii fanɛ mbronito bee liɛ abar 
nna.
Kasɔbii be Asɔkpra
1. Bɛ atere nɛ ntilemu be kasibɛ be mbra be ekpa so n kuu mmalgafol.
2. Bɛ adulwiso be kasibɛ be mbra be ekpa so n kuu mmalgafol.
3. Bɛ ashuŋso nɛ adelgeso be kasibɛ be mbra be ekpa so n kuu mmalgafol.
Alakal Tenini
• Atere bee shuŋ ewɔrɔpo, esɔpo tanyuso nɛ esɔpo tangelge be kushuŋ, 
ketere delgesobi nɛ kamalgafolshiŋ be kumu be kushuŋ.
• Ntilemu gba bee shuŋ ewɔrɔpo nɛ esɔpo be kushuŋ kekuu mmalgafol to.
• Adulwiso bee delge atere so nna. Amo e naa junkpar atere monɛ a bee 
delge so na saŋɛ damta ashi Ngbanyato.
• Ashuŋso bee delge kesheŋwɔrɔ nko kananɛ kusɔ nko kesheŋ la so nna. 
Ngbanyato, kushuŋso be keta n shuŋ maa bɛ asɔ be kananɛ a sa so. Anyee 
ta atere nɛ ashuŋso nna a shuŋ a kɔr ama amo nɛ ntilemu baa shuŋ bre, a 
bee shuŋ kɔnɔkoŋwuleso nna.
• Adelgeso bee delge ashuŋso so nna n ka beeŋ tiŋ n delge amo braana 
adelgeso gba so.

kelijima n ta atuwebi na n ŋini eŋinipo.

d. Keterefolshiŋ be kumu: atere beeŋ tiŋ ba fanɛ keterefolshiŋ be kumu. 
Keni ade:
i. Aklembi kɔ yawu ga.
ii. Ebu pupɔr na bee tushi.
iii. Anye wɔ epe.
iv. Kowu gboŋ ko tɔr kabre.
2. Jande baa deso: Mbra monɛ bu kɔ a ta ntilemu a kuu mmalgafol kɔr abarto 
ashi Ghana be ngbarana to nna.
 Amo kikɛ to, ntilemu bee shuŋ fanɛ:
a. Ewɔrɔpo ashi mmalgafol to. Keni ade:
i. N yɔ sukuru.
ii. Anye bee keni avidiyo tarukama.
iii. Bu mushe kagbenefuliso.

b. Ntilemu gba bee shuŋ fanɛ esɔpo ashi mmalgafol to (esɔpo tanyuso nɛ 
esɔpo tangelge). Keni amobe akeniso kaseto ere:
i. Samaakuse wu bumo. (esɔpo tanyuso)
ii. Amaabaŋɛ ta klembi n sa mo. (esɔpo tangelge)
iii. Amaabaŋɛ sa mo klembi. (esɔpo tangelge)
iv. Eŋinipo na sa anye epe be kushuŋ. (esɔpo tanyuso)
Kushuŋ
1. Ŋinito ketere n shin sa fanɛ akeniso kudu. Chige ketuwebi na to n sa 
bebiipo kikɛ ebiikpa.
2. Kunyɔnyɔto, menye e sibɛ atere be ashuŋ anyɔ n nase. Menye e daŋɛ 
benyɔ ko so nɛ menyebe katuŋ e bir kumobe kelijima.
3. Ŋinito katilemu n shin sa fanɛ akeniso kudu. Chige ketuwebi na to n sa 
bebiipo kikɛ ebiikpa.
4. a. Kraŋ kaseto be kebɔaya ere nɛ menyebe ntuŋana to, menye e pin 
atere nɛ ntilemu kumo to.
b. Ta atere nɛ menye pin na be anu n kuu mmalgafol birabarso. Blase 
nɛ fo chige fobe ketuwebi to n sa bebiipo kikɛ ebiikpa.
c. Ta ntilemu nɛ menye pin na be anu n kuu mmalgafol birabarso. 
Blase nɛ fo chige fobe ketuwebi to n sa bebiipo kikɛ.
Njɔnɔ
Njɔnɔ la asɔbɔaya nɛ ekama nyi nɛnɛ nna nɛ bu gbugi a la anyebe asɔbɔaya-
teriana durnyaŋ kikɛ to. A kɔ nnembi damta nɛ amobe eyerto be kapɔr, adabi nɛ 
kayerwule kɔr abarto. A la aya ana wuraana nna nɛ amo niopibiana la ajinkaamu 
nɛ a wɔ kupuŋto. Saŋɛ na ebi ka daŋ bla jinkaamu a ji kekpaŋ so, a daŋ chɛrga 
amobe kebawɔtɔ nna m bɛ bomin so n taga baasa to. A bee wɔrɔ asɔ ga a pin 
dimedi be kebawɔtɔ fanɛ kasha, kanyaŋ nɛ kufuu n saa bɛ amo so loŋ. Adamtato, 
njɔnɔ bee gberge efɛ ga. Amobe asoe naa nu ga a tiŋ a nu awor be yiri kikɛ kufɔ. 
Kusɔnɛ ku shinɛ njɔnɔ kɔ kasha ga ela fanɛ feeŋ tiŋ bla amo nɛ a baa shuŋ ashuŋ 
damta. Kechɛto be njɔnɔ beeŋ tiŋ chɛ atanpo to karɛchɛkama, loŋ nɛ kebawɔtɔ be 
njɔnɔ bee tiŋ a lulo baasa monɛ bu wɔ kayernyaŋ to. Bu naa kɔ njɔnɔ a yɔ kafin 
nɛ kemɔlwɔ baasa to n saa gberge efɛ nɛ kushuŋsɔ maaŋ tiŋ. Asɔ lɛla nɛ njɔnɔ 
bee wɔrɔ ere be jaga, amobe nkpa maŋ wɔnteŋ fanɛ mfɛ kudu n yɔ mfɛ kudu anu

1. Pin mmalgaba monɛ amobe nseto chaŋ na be ashuŋ. Ta fobe atuwebi n

APUNTOSƆ
Menye teŋ bii adulwiso be asheŋ. Nɛ ntuŋ so, menye e ta adulwiso asa monɛ 
menyeeŋ ta n kuu mmalgafol n delge ade so:
a. Fobe ebiikpabu
b. Fo teri kpakpaso
c. Fobe sukuru be kulɔnde
d. Fobe kanaŋ
‘Kedulwiso’ la kamalgaba nna nɛ ku bee buwito nko a delge ketere so. Bu kɔ 
adulwiso nna a delge esa nko kusɔ ko be kapɔr so nko n ta a karga kusɔ pɔtɛ so.
Jande baa deso: Ngbar kama nɛ kananɛ kumobe adulwiso du. Keni ade:
a. Awundre bee sha alaŋ dra.
b. Kebinyɛnsobi na du tenteŋ n shin wɔlso.
c. Amaabaŋɛ du wɔrɛwɔrɛbi achɔ mo siponyɛn.
Ashi (a) to, “dra” bee delgeso nko a buwito alaŋ be dubi monɛ emalgapo na bee 
sha nna. Ashi (b) to, “tenteŋ” nɛ “wɔlso” bee delge kebinyɛnsobi na be kapɔr so 
nna. Ashi (c) to, bu ta “wɔrɛwɔrɛbi” na nna n ta Amaabaŋɛ nɛ mo siponyɛn be 
kanyiasheŋ a kesar abar.
Adulwiso be mbra/ashuŋ
Mbra monɛ bu kɔ a ta adulwiso a kuu mmalgafol kɔr abarto nna ashi Ghana be 
ngbarana to.
Amobe adamta to, adulwiso bee shuŋ Ngbanyato fanɛ:
1. Ku bee delge ketere so ashi kamalgafol to nna. Keni ade:
a. Gbaŋɛ nyɔso na bee shile achɔ ade na kikɛ.
b. N wu kowu gboŋgboŋi.
2. A bee bɛ atere monɛ a bee delgeso na so nna. Keni ade:
a. Kowu nyɔso na tɔr.
b. Keche gboŋ ko yɔ epe.
Menye daŋ bii adulwiso be ntuŋso kamanto ndoŋ. Amobe akeniso ko e wɔ kaseto 
ere na:

 Baasa damta fara a pin kananɛ anyebe kebawɔtɔsheŋ bee tɔrɔ anyebe 
achambɔ. Achambɔ be kekuŋ daga ku ka la kesheŋ kpra nna n sa anye 
kikɛ. Ama baasa gberɛ e kɔ kenyi gberɛ ta n laŋɛ achambɔ be kekeniso 
nɛnɛ. Anyebe shɛŋ be kemaŋ wɔtɔ be kebawɔtɔ e naa daŋɛso a jajɛ 
anyebe achambɔ ere karɛchɛkama. Fanɛ epi be kelɛ jagajaga, epi be 
kelɛ, arɔba be kelɛ, nɛ anye maŋ yige le be kebawɔtɔ lubi, jimani ko beeŋ 
ba nɛ echefoso be mbia beeŋ ji awurfoŋ nkpal anyebe ku ta asheŋ a pel 
so. Amoso ku la kprɛmɛ nna n sa ma nɛ fo nɛ anye e wɔrɔ kenishipre n 
kuŋ anyebe achambɔ. Ku la anyebe kushuŋ/tileshi kpra nna nɛ anye e 
shuŋ/bɛso n kuŋ anyebe kenanasawule/Ebɔrɛ be kakɛ gboŋ ere. Anyebe 
adabi lubi ta n laŋɛ achambɔ be kapliɛ be jerbɛ ela nchu be keji anye, 
adɔɔjibi be kemaa wɔrɔ nɛnɛ.

ASHUŊSO
Keta ashuŋso nɛ adelgeso a kuu mmalgafol ashi Ghana be ngbarana to kɔ mbra 
monɛ anyee bɛso nna. Le be mbra e na chɛto nɛ kasibɛ na bee lar anishi a sa nɛ 
ekraŋpo na bee pin kebɔaya na be kefiito nɛnɛ. Kebaa ta Ghana be ngbarana be 
mbra ashuŋ fobe kasibɛ to bee sa na nɛ fee kuu mmalgafol monɛ a kɔ kefiito nɛnɛ 
Ngbanyato.
Pɔɛ nɛ anye e bii mbra na, anye e palto kusɔ monɛ ku la kushuŋso to. Keni akeniso 
monɛ a wɔ kaseto ere. Mmalgaba monɛ a nyɔɔ a chɔ amo braana na la ashuŋso 
nna.
1. Edɔɔpo na bee buse mobe kadɔɔ na saŋɛ kikɛ.
2. Mbia na bee nite a yɔ sukuru nna Alijima kama.
3. Anye bee tɛto kachipurso kikɛ nna a saŋɛ anyebe eyur to.
Kushuŋso ela kamalgaba nko kamalgafolshiŋ monɛ bu kɔ a ŋini kesheŋwɔrɔ. 
Kushuŋso la kamalgafol be ewɔrɔpo na be kaba nna. Kuma, kumo ela kamalgafol 
be ewɔrɔpo na be kumu.
Kebaa ta ashuŋso be mbra a shuŋ mmalgafol to
Kebaa ta ashuŋso be mbra a shuŋ mmalgafol to kɔr abarto ashi Ghana be ngbarana

a. Jɔnɔ na bee gbu kekuloŋ na ase saŋɛkama.
 Mfa, kushuŋso gbu bee kaŋɛ anye na kusɔ monɛ ewɔrɔpo “jɔnɔ na” bee 
wɔrɔ kekuloŋ na ase.
b. Bebiipo na bee dii cheche nna a yɔ sukuru chipurso kikɛ.
 Kushuŋso dii bee kaŋɛ anye na kusɔ monɛ ewɔrɔpo “bebiipo na” wɔrɔ.
2. kushuŋso bee kaŋɛ anye na kananɛ ewɔrɔpo na du kamalgafol na to. Fanɛ:
 Koji nya kagbenefuli mobe nsulwe na be lalaluwe.
 Mfa, kushuŋso nya bee kaŋɛ anye kananɛ ewɔrɔpo “Koji na” du na nsulwe 
na be lalaluwe.
3. Kushuŋso bee shuŋ fanɛ kamalgafol be ewɔrɔpo na be kumu na. Fanɛ
a. Ekuloŋ potiibi na bee shile eleŋso.

Fo nyiŋi asɔ monɛ a la adelgeso?
Adelgeso la mmalgaba nko mmalgabafolshiŋ nna nɛ a bee buwito kushuŋso nko 
kumo barkasa kedelgeso ko so a ŋini kaboŋ, saŋɛ, eyilikpa nɛ adamta. Adelgeso

3. Bɔl be katuŋ na pel nɛ kagbenefuli. (kananɛ)

KASOTOFUTI
Kaba ere bee kenito Kasibɛbirabarso be ntuŋso nna. Kasibɛbirabarso la kenyikpra 
nna n sa Ghana be ngbarana nɛ kasɔbii pɔtɛana kikɛ fanɛ Mbronito.
Ta n ya fo kumuba ere be lalaluwe, feeŋ tiŋ:
1. Sibɛ kesheŋkute be Kasibɛbirabarso.
2. sibɛ kedelgeso be kasibɛbirabarso
3. sibɛ kebuwiasheŋto be kasibɛbirabarso.
Kasɔbiikpra
• Kasibɛbirabarso la kasibɛ monɛ ku bee lara kesheŋ ko nko kesheŋtirso ko 
efuli nna.
• Feeŋ bii kasibɛbirabarso be ntuŋ sa mfa:
o Kesheŋkute la kasibɛ tenteŋ be keshɛrkpaŋ sibɛso nna nɛ ku bee bɛ 
kesheŋkute be kapɔrto be ekpa so a lara esa be mfɛra efuli.
o Kedelgeso be kasibɛbirabarso la kasibɛbirabarso be katuŋ monɛ ku 
bee shinɛ ebiipo bee delgeso/folwe kusɔ so nna: kusɔ, esa, kaboŋ, 
mfɛra, kagbene be afɛso nɛ adamta.
o Kebuwiasheŋto be kasibɛbirabarso la kasibɛbirabarso monɛ ku bee 
buwito nko a delge kusɔ so nna. Ku bee buwito kumu na, ekpaana nko 
lakal to be asheŋ nɛ a bee lar anishi nɛnɛ.
• Kasibɛbirabarso kama kɔ kumo nawule be kapɔr nɛ ayabi nna.

Kasibɛbirabarso
Agoni kpra ko e daga nɛ fo baa ko n tiŋ sibɛ kasibɛbirabarso lɛla. A daga fo ka 
nase fobe asheŋtirso na nɛnɛ nɛ nto. Feeŋ wɔrɔ le nɛ kebaa ta abɔaya monɛ a duli a 
bar n wɔtɔ katuŋ koŋwule to, kekute esoso/chipurso be asheŋ pɔɛ kaseto/kanyiso, 
a lara kashinteŋ efuli, akasar asɔ abar nɛ adamta.
Kasibɛbirabarso la kasibɛ monɛ ku bee lara kesheŋ ko nko kesheŋtirso ko efuli

Kasibɛbirabarso be ntuŋso be asheŋ nɛ anye beeŋ ji mfa n fara nɛ kesheŋkute 
be kasibɛbirabarso.
Kesheŋkute be kasibɛbirabarso
Kesheŋkute la kasibɛ tenteŋ be keshɛrkpaŋ sibɛso nna nɛ ku bee bɛ kesheŋkute be 
kapɔrto be ekpa so a ta kumu ko a lara esa be anishi be awuso efuli. Ku beeŋ tiŋ 
ala kashinteŋ nko efɛ. Saŋɛ damta esa koŋwule be katilemu nɛ ku bee ta a shuŋ. 
Saŋɛ choŋso be mmalgaba nɛ alakalfoni nɛ kamalganyi be apɔrsobi gba la asɔ nɛ 
a bee chɛto nna a pɛ esa be lakal a wɔtɔ keshɛrkpaŋ na to.
Kesheŋkute be kasibɛbirabarso be amu ko nde:
• Sibɛ keshɛrkpaŋ ta n laŋɛ fo sososo be sukuru be keyɔ be kachɛ be asheŋ.
• Sibɛ keshɛrkpaŋ ta n laŋɛ fobe ewushi be saŋɛ monɛ fo maaŋ teŋso.
• Sibɛ keshɛrkpaŋ ta n laŋɛ fobe kanyɛ/kusɔwɔrɔso monɛ fobe kagbene fuli 
ga so.

Adaŋkaresheŋ
KASOTOFUTI
Kaba ere bee lara efuli Ghana be ayiri be ketumbayasheŋ nna a laŋɛ fobe daŋkare 
to be agbartere be elerkpa. Ku beeŋ chɛ fo to nɛ fo pin kusɔnɛ ku bee bra agbartere 
nɛ amobe atunɔ. Kasɔbii ere bee leŋ fo to nna nɛ fo delge ketere sa be ekpaana 
be kepinto n shin bunyaŋ fo ka shi Ghana na to, kumobe adaŋkare nɛ ataada 
nɛ enɔgboŋ anyɔ. Kaba ere na malga kebir n wɔtɔ kenimuya to (ketumbaya) be 
asheŋ nna. Kelijima na beeŋ ba laŋɛ ekpaana monɛ adaga pɔɛ nɛ bu fara kawɔrɔ, 
kawɔrɔ gbagba nɛ kumobe lalaluwe ashi fobe daŋkare nɛ Ghana be ngbar pɔtɛana 
kikɛ be adaŋkare to. Feeŋ naŋ bii atunɔ monɛ kawɔrɔ na kɔ n sa kebifɔlbi na, 
mobe kanaŋ nɛ kade na kikɛ. Adaga fo ka tiŋ m buwito Ghana be ngbar pɔtɛana 
be ketumbayasheŋ be amo nɛ a duli abar nɛ amobe mbarga to.
Ta n ya fo kumuba ere be lalaluwe, feeŋ tiŋ:
• Migto agbartere be elerkpa n shin tise amo to nɛnɛ.
• Malga mbifɔlbi be kebir n wɔtɔ kenimuto (ketumbaya) be ekpaana be 
asheŋ. (pɔɛ nɛ bu fara, kawɔrɔ nɛ kumobe keluweto)
• Ta Ghana to be adaŋkare be ekpaana be kebir n wɔtɔ kenimuto (ketumbaya) 
n kasar abarso n keni.
Kasɔbiikpra
• Agbartere bee shi kegbar ko kutɔ nna.
• Amo nɛ asɔtooso lempo e naa liɛ abar.
• A bee ŋini baasa nɛ baa ji amo na kananɛ bumo nɛ adaŋkare liɛ abar nna.
• Ketumbaya la saŋɛ monɛ mbifɔlbi fo kakurwe nna.
3
KABA 6 AGBARTERE NƐ KETUMBAYASHEŊ BE KAWƆRƆ
• Ketumbaya be kawɔrɔ ela kebir esa n wɔtɔ kachina to.
• Baa wɔrɔ ketumbayasheŋ nna a sa benyɛn nɛ beche kikɛ.
AGBARTERE
Atere ko wɔtɔ nna nɛ anyee ji amo nkpal anye nɛ asɔtooso lempo ko ka liɛ abar 
so. Le be atere nɛ baa tere agbartere. Pɔɛ nɛ fo kraŋ agbartere be asheŋ, adaga fo 
ka pin asɔ nɛ agbar la.
Manɛ ela Agbar?
Ade la agbarnyɛnso nko agbarcheso nna. Agbar la asɔtooso lempo nna nɛ bumo 
nɛ bu yɛrda fanɛ a kɔ eleŋ ko a kuŋ bumobe asheŋwɔrɔso ko bee bunyaŋ nko a 
shuŋ amo. Agbar kɔ ayoyul, bunyaŋ nɛ kebɛso be eleŋ nna. Amo nɛ kabɔrɛshuŋ 
be yɛrda nɛ kebɛsopoya e naa liɛ abar. A beeŋ tiŋ a la becheso nko benyɛnso. 
Amobe ako be akeniso ela Zeus, Apollo, Athena, Aphrodite, Artemis, nɛ adamta. 
Ashi Ghana to kabɔrɛshuŋ nko ngbar kama kɔ agbar monɛ bu yɛrda nna. Ghana 
be agbar monɛ a gbugi be ako ela:
Ngbanya: Sɔnyɔŋ be Kipo, Chama be Lansa, Busunu be Gbulo, Jukuku be 
Chembi/Lempo, Chɛrmboe be Lata, Jindeyu, Jebuni, nɛ adamta.
Nkraŋto: Dantu, Nae, Sakumɔ, Kɔɔle, Klote, La Kpa nɛ adamta
Mbɔŋto: Kune, Tegare, Nyamaa, nɛ adamta.
Nwɔŋto: Tambo, Gurigbaya, Jaagbo nɛ adamta.
Agbar mo a gbugi fobe efuliso?
Agbartere
Baa sa baasa agbartere nna nkpal kananɛ bu lar nɛ bumobe yɛrda so. Agbartere 
naa la atere monɛ mbuna ko, nde ko nko adaŋkare ko nawule bee ji nna nkpal 
kananɛ bu liɛ loŋ be agbar na so.
Agbartere ko
Ade la agbartere be akeniso ko nna ashi Ghanaebi to:
1. Ashi Mbɔtɔɔ to, Anloebi nɛ bu wɔ V olta be efuliso na bee shuŋ kegbar ko 
nɛ baa tere ‘Afa’ nɛ ku la nkpal be kegbir nɛ ekpalpo na la ‘Bokɔ’ nɛ mobe 
sososo be kebinyɛnso bee ji ‘Amuzu’.
4
KABA 6 AGBARTERE NƐ KETUMBAYASHEŊ BE KAWƆRƆ
2. Ashi Mbɔŋ to, kegbar kama nɛ kumobe kachɛ nɛ ku liɛ nna. Amoso bɔkwɛ 
to be kachɛ monɛ bu kurwe esa e naa ŋini ketere monɛ baaŋ sa mo. ‘Adwo’ 
la Atania be kegbar nna loŋso ‘Adwoa’ la ketere nɛ baa sa eche nɛ bu kurwe 
Atania achɛ nna nɛ ‘Kwadzo’ la enyɛn peya.
Wɔrɔ ania n tere esoso be agbartere ere n keni. Shinɛ eŋinipo e keni fanɛ fo tere 
amo nɛnɛ aa. Fo nyi agbartere ko be akeniso fobe efuliso aa?
Agbartere be elerkpa:
Agbartere be elerkpa kɔr abarto n shin bɛ baasa monɛ ba ji amo na be yɛrda nɛ 
adaŋkare so nna. Ashi Mbɔtɔɔ to, agbartere be elerkpa ela Yeʋe (bɔrɛ be keponte 
be kegbar), Mbɔŋ peya bee shi nchu be agbar to nna nɛ Dangme peya ko shi 
kakurwe be agbar to.
Fo nyi fobe ketere be elerkpa?
Kusɔ monɛ ku bee bra agbartere
Baasa bee ji agbartere nna nkpal asɔ damta so. Baaŋ tiŋ ta kegbartere n sa esa nɛ 
ku baa delge kegbar na be ashuŋ so, nɛ baa sa ako malɛ nkpal kegbar na be kekpal 
be kapɔr so. Ako malɛ beeŋ tiŋ a la keleŋto monɛ baa nyɛ kegbar na to, ako malɛ 
wɔtɔ a lara efuli na be daŋkare efuli nko amonɛ a bee ŋini kegbar na be kapɔr nɛ 
kumobe awɔrɔbi.
N naaŋ ta n tiiso, eche nɛ enyɛn baa fin kakurwe a gben, baa yɔ kegbar to nna n 
ya kule kanyɛ. Baa bɔ ntaŋ nna n shin nase kebia na kegbar na be ketere nkpal 
ntaŋ na so.
Agbartere be tunɔ
Agbartere kɔ tunɔ damta ashi anyebe abɔrɛshumpo be kebawɔtɔ to.
Atunɔ monɛ agbartere wuraana bee nyɛ nde:
1. Kepin manaŋmanaŋ. Agbartere bee chɛto nɛ anyee pin kegbar monɛ esa bee 
shuŋ nɛ kakpa nɛ esa shi.
2. A bee ŋini kananɛ esa na nɛ kegbar na liɛ abar nna.
3. Agbartere la kapitɛ nna nɛ bedrapo nyeshi n sa kamantoebi nɛ a bee kuŋ 
adaŋkare.
4. Ku bee ŋini ketere na wura mo nawurana be yɛrda nna.
5. Ashi ayɛrda ko to, bu yɛrda fanɛ kebaa ji kegbartere bee sa eleŋ, kekuŋ nɛ 
keyoyul to be kenimu nna.

KABA 6 AGBARTERE NƐ KETUMBAYASHEŊ BE KAWƆRƆ
KETUMBAYASHEŊ BE KAWƆRƆ
Kaba ere bee ji kebir mbifɔlbi n wɔtɔ kenimuya to nna a laŋɛ a yɔ ekpaana, 
asɔwɔrɔso monɛ baa wɔrɔ pɔɛ nɛ bu fara kawɔrɔ, kawɔrɔ gbagba nɛ kumobe 
lalaluwe ashi adaŋkare pɔtɛana to.
Mfɛra be mbishi:
Feeŋ tiŋ nyiŋi eyur so be nchɛrga kikɛ nɛ fee wu fobe mfɛ kudu n yɔ kudu ana be 
kefito aa?
Manɛ ela ketumbaya?
Saŋɛ ere la kebawɔtɔ to be jimanɛ monɛ kebinyɛnsobi nko kebichesobi bee daŋ 
a kii enyɛn nko eche monɛ e beeŋ tiŋ kurwe. Ku la kusɔ monɛ mbichesobi peya 
bee fara mfɛ kudu n yɔ mfɛ kudu ana to nna nɛ mbinyɛnsobi malɛ bee fara mfɛ 
kuduanyɔ n yɔ mfɛ kuduashe to. (ama buko peya bee kaa wɔrɔ manaŋ nko a chɛr 
pɔɛ a wɔrɔ)
Mbichesobi be kapɔrto be nchɛrga
Nchɛrga monɛ bu peshe mbichesobi to be ako beeŋ tiŋ a la:
• Aleŋto bee buwito nna
• Abembi/abɛŋ bee daŋ a tiiso
• Afiimu na bee kii kulkulbi
• Baa nyɛ bumobe sososo be eyurpi/ntaman
• Anyipo be kegbul/kekɔr
• Abaatofuibi nɛ ngbaga be kejɔ/kekɔr
Mbinyɛnsobi be kapɔrto be nchɛrga
Mbinyɛnsobi be nchɛrga monɛ anyeeŋ tiŋ peshe be ako beeŋ tiŋ a la:
• Kututu nɛ awɔlbi be kedaŋ
• Abaatofuibi nɛ ngbaga be kekɔr
• Kagbene nɛ abatimu be kepargato
• Eblaŋnyifu be kedaŋ
• Ebol be kekii chiŋgliŋ
• Nteŋ be kedaŋɛso
• Anishito be afuibi/katol be kekɔr
Asɔ ere bee ŋini nkpa to be saŋɛ nɛ baa tere Ketumba nna.

Ketumbayasheŋ la daŋkare be kebulɔso nna nɛ baa ta esa a bulɔso nɛ ku bee 
ŋini mobe kelar kebia to n luri kenimuya to. Kede la kawɔrɔ nko daŋkare be 
kesheŋwɔrɔ monɛ ku bɛ ketere be kesa so nna a lara kebinyɛnsobi nko kebichesobi 
ashi kebia to a yɔ kenimuya to.
Shabɔrɛ 6.1 kaseto ere bee ŋini kananɛ Ghana be ngbarana ko bee tere 
ketumbayasheŋ be kawɔrɔ na.

Nuso nɛ ba tere ketumbayasheŋ fobe daŋkare to? Benyɛn nɛ beche kikɛ bee bulɔ 
kumo so aa? Manɛ ela ketumbaya be kawɔrɔ?
Kebir n wɔtɔ la kebulɔso nna nɛ baa ta esa a bulɔ a ŋini kachinato be eyilikpa 
be nchɛrga. Baaŋ tiŋ m bir esa n wɔtɔ mamachi be ashuŋ to, ashiri be ntuŋ to nko 
kabɔrɛshuŋ ko to. Ama kebir n wɔtɔ monɛ anyee bir kumobe kelijima ere la kebir 
kebifɔlbi n wɔtɔ kenimuya to nɛ baa tere ketumbayasheŋ na nna.
Ketumbayasheŋ be ekpaana
Nkpal adaŋkare ka kɔr abarto so, ekpaana monɛ yiri kikɛ bee bulɔso a wɔrɔ kawɔrɔ 
ere gba maaŋ ba la kukoŋwule. Keblase monɛ baa wɔrɔ pɔɛ nɛ bu fara, kawɔrɔ 
gbagba nɛ kumobe lalaluwe nɛ bu delgeso kaseto ere na.

KABA 6 AGBARTERE NƐ KETUMBAYASHEŊ BE KAWƆRƆ
Keta Ketumbayasheŋ N Kasar Abarso: Amo Nɛ A 
Duli Abar Nko A La Kukoŋwule
Beche be ketumbayasheŋ
1. Pɔɛ nɛ ku fara
 Benawuraana baaŋ ya wu nchɛrga ko ashi mbifɔlbi cheso to, baa fara keblase 
ko nna.
 Saŋɛ damta, kebichesobi na baaŋ ya wu mobe sososo be eyurpi/ntaman, baa 
bulɔso ekpaana ere be ako nna:
a. Sososo, baa barga mbichesobi na nna ashi bumobe nnaŋebi to nɛ bu bla 
bumo ase a jo ketumbayasheŋ na.
b. Kebichesobi na be baasa beeŋ kaŋɛ benimu na nko baasa monɛ baa wɔrɔ 
kawɔrɔ na bumobe mfɛra.
c. Bechenimu beeŋ kuŋ mbichesobi na n wɔtɔ ebu koŋwule to n shin buwi 
bumo kenishi ta n laŋɛ adabi monɛ adaga eche monɛ e fo kakil ka kɔ nɛ 
e tiŋ n kata mobe laŋ nɛnɛ.
d. Baaŋ ŋini bumo laŋ be kekata be ashuŋ fanɛ kadaŋɛ, kafuwe, kafɔr, 
farfarbi nɛ adamta.
e. Baa ŋini bumo enɔto be ashuŋ fanɛ klaŋ be kalɔ, ashembi be kawɔrɔ nɛ 
adamta na.
f. Bu naa bii kananɛ baa cha n saa boŋ adaŋkare be nshɛ na.
g. Baa ŋini bumo kananɛ adaga bu ba kata bumobe amu keche nɛ kenyɛn 
be kegama be kabaso nna saŋɛ nɛ bu kaaŋ kil.
2. Kawɔrɔ na be saŋɛ/gbagba
 Kawɔrɔ na to, echenimu nko esa nɛ e bee wɔrɔ kumo na bee wɔrɔ bumo 
kaseto be asɔ ere nna.
 E bee blase nna n shin too nchu n ta mbia na n bɔɔ agbar enɔ nɛ kawɔrɔ na e 
tiŋ yɔ so nɛnɛ. Kachutoo na be kaman, baa ta bumo nna a bulɔ adaŋkare ere 
so:
a. Keyoyul to be kechɔnkeni fanɛ e kraa la tumba. Baa sa nɛ kebia na bee 
china kejembu nyɔɔso so nna, a bɛr lor to nko kupɔ to, nɛ adamta.
b. Esa na naa she bumobe amu nna.
c. Mbia na bee china kabɛbi nko kawolbi so nna kawɔrɔ ere be saŋɛ.

KABA 6 AGBARTERE NƐ KETUMBAYASHEŊ BE KAWƆRƆ
Kawɔrɔ na be kaman
• Kawɔrɔ na be lalaluwe, benimu pupɔr na nɛ bumobe kanaŋ nɛ beteri beeŋ 
nite n kulti n churɔ kade na ebi.
• Kade na to ebi bee sa benimu pupɔr na nkɛ nna a wɔrɔ bumo ansaŋ nɛ kumu 
lɛla bu ka tiŋ wɔrɔ kawɔrɔ na nɛnɛ. Nkɛ na be ako beeŋ tiŋ a la amanshɛrbi, 
ashembi, asɔbuuso, achimu nɛ adamta.

be kawɔrɔ na be lalaluwe be amfoni
Keta Ketumbayasheŋ n Kasar Abar:
Mbarga monɛ a wɔ Ghana be adaŋkareana be kawɔrɔ to.
Adaŋkareana na be kawɔrɔ monɛ a duli abar na be bushi, ako wɔtɔ nɛ a la adaŋkare 
ko nawule peya nɛ anyeeŋ bir amobe kelijima kaseto ere.
Mbɔtɔɔ be baasa
1. Ashi kade na nɛ kusɔ mo so nɛ ba wɔrɔ kawɔrɔ na, kawɔrɔ na beeŋ tiŋ n ji 
fanɛ bɔkwɛ koŋwule n ya fo kufol koŋwule.
2. Baa kuŋ bumo na n wɔtɔ laŋ gbagba na be kaman n shin kaŋɛ bumo teriana 
nɛ bu ba wɔ bumo kutɔ a deŋi bumo anishi le be saŋɛ ere.
3. Kawɔrɔ na to, kefule daŋɛso na be keji bee ŋini kakurwe nna.

KABA 6 AGBARTERE NƐ KETUMBAYASHEŊ BE KAWƆRƆ
Krobo be baasa
1. Jimanɛ nɛ bu baŋ yili Kasawule be kegbar (Nene Kloweki) be katilemu n bir 
kawɔrɔ na be kebomboŋ na nɛ Kroboebi bee wɔrɔ ketumbayasheŋ (Dipo) 
a sa mbichesobi. Mbroni be kufol nyɔsepo to nɛ ba wɔrɔ kumo nɛ ku bee ji 
nchɛnu.
2. Pɔɛ nɛ kawɔrɔ na e fara, mbichesobi na bumo nawuraana bee ta bumo nna 
a sa bumobe kabuna be enimu monɛ e bee wɔrɔ ‘Dipo’ na.
3. Kawɔrɔ na to, enimu na bee too nchu nna n shin wɔrɔ ademansheŋ damta n 
sa bumo hali bumobe amu be kaseto be kashe, kechina nwol so nɛ adamta.
Nkraŋ be baasa
1. Nkraŋ bee wɔrɔ Otofo nna kebichesobi na ka du fimbi nko saŋɛ kama nɛ ku 
ba yili fanɛ bu wɔrɔ kumo.
Mbɔŋ be baasa

Daŋkare be Kejunkpar (Kewuraji)
KASOTOFUTI
Kaba ere bee futi fobe kusoe nna ta n laŋɛ Ghana be efuliso be daŋkare be 
kejunkpar be kapɔr. Ku bee buwito baasa monɛ bu wɔ daŋkare be kejunkpar be 
kapɔr to nɛ bumobe atunɔ nna. Kaba ere bee sha kesa fo kenyi nɛ kepinto ta n 
laŋɛ fobe daŋkare to be kejunkpar be kapɔrto be kabaso nna. Feeŋ pin daŋkare 
be bejunkparpo be ashuŋ nɛ bumobe ashuŋ na be atunɔ ta n laŋɛ fobe kadeto be 
baasa be kebawɔtɔ lɛla nɛ nkilgi be kabaso.
Ta nɛ kumu ere a fo ekar, feeŋ tiŋ
i. Migeto daŋkare be kejunkpar (kewuraji) be kapɔrto (etuto, kanaŋ be 
enimu, kabuna be enimu).
ii Migeto daŋkare be kejunkpar (kewuraji) be kapɔrto (ewura, bewurbi, 
begboŋipo nɛ bedamta).
Alakal Tenini
• Etuto ela kanaŋ monɛ ku la enyɛn nɛ mobe eche nɛ mbia be kanaŋ be 
enimu(kumu), (kakpa nɛ kanaŋ na bɛ etuto na be kenana be kebor so nna 
na.
• Kanaŋ monɛ ku bɛ eche be kenana be kebor so bre, eche(enio) beeŋ tiŋ a 
la kanaŋ na be enimu(kumu).
• Mboŋ ko bre, kabuna be benimu la daŋkare be efuli be bewura nna nɛ 
benimu bee lara bumo a china ndoŋ.

DAŊKARE BE KEJUNKPAR (KEWURAJI) 
BE KAPƆR
Migeto daŋkare be kejunkpar (kewuraji) be kapɔrto (etuto, kanaŋ be enimu, 
kabuna be enimu).
Daŋkare be kejunkpar
Daŋkare be kejunkpar la kejunkpar be katuŋ ko nna nɛ bu kɔ dra be kenyiasheŋ 
nɛ abar be kechɛto be ekpaana a shuŋ. Daŋkare be kejunkpar monɛ ku wɔ Ghana 
be ndeana to kɔ kebɛso-kebɛso be kapɔr lɛla nna. Ngbar/yiri kikɛ nɛ bumobe 
kapɔr nna ama mboŋ damta be kapɔr bee duli abar nna.
Kanaŋ to be Kejunkpar be kapɔr
Ashi Ghana to, kanaŋ beeŋ tiŋ a la kanaŋ tutiya nɛ ku kɔ etuto, enio nɛ mbia 
nawule nko kanaŋ gboŋ nɛ ku la kanaŋ tutiya na nɛ beniopibiana fanɛ benana, 
bewɔpa, betana/beniokar/beniogboŋ, bechɛlpo nɛ bedamta. Kede anyebe mfɛra 
to, daŋkare be kejunkpar be kapɔr ashi kanaŋ to kɔ etuto, kanaŋ be enimu, kabuna 
be enimu, bewura, bewurabi, begboŋipo nɛ bewura tɔgmase, nɛ bumo nɛ bu ka.
Kushuŋ
Nuso ela fo kadeto be daŋkare be kejunkpar be kapɔr? Wanɛ e naa junkpar 
fobe kanaŋ tutiya? Wanɛ e naa junkpar fobe kanaŋ buwitoso? Fo daŋɛ kabuna 
so aa?
Kebɛso-kebɛso be shabɔrɛ la shabɔrɛ monɛ ku bee ŋini kananɛ katuŋ be kapɔrto 
du nna. Ku bee ŋini benimu nɛ bumobe beyaasepo be kananɛ bu bɛ abar so nna.
Daŋkare be kejunkpar be kabaso ashi epe, kebɛso-kebɛso be shabɔrɛ beeŋ ba du 
fanɛ kede;

KABA 7 Adaŋkare be Kawɔrɔ nɛ Daŋkare be Kejunkpar (Kewuraji)
Fig7.1: Kebɛso-kebɛso be shabɔrɛ ashi laŋto:
1. Kabuna be enimu:
 Kabuna la baasa nɛ bu kɔ kenana koŋwule nna nko bumo nɛ kakil bra bumo 
abarso. Bu la nnaŋ be katuŋ nna nɛ bu kɔ kenanafofo koŋwule n saa kɔ 
enimu koŋwule nɛ ketere koŋwule. Adabi nko lakal koŋwule e na bra bumo 
abarso. Esa nɛ baasa ere bee lara fanɛ e junkpar bumo nɛ ba tere kabuna be 
enimu. Ashi adaŋkare ko to, kabuna na to be nnaŋ wurbi na be benimu e na 
kaa chala a lara kabuna be enimu. Beko malɛ kenimu so nɛ ku bee bɛ so.
2. Kanaŋ be benimu:
 Kanaŋ be enimu ela esa nɛ bu lara fanɛ e junkpar kanaŋ na. Bumobe kushuŋ 
ela kanaŋ na be kekuŋ nɛ kumobe kadigal be yulwe be kafin. Adaga bu ka 
kɔ kejunkpar be adabi ko. Saŋɛ damta, enyɛn nɛ baa lara nɛ e bee junkpar 
kanaŋ.
3. Etuto
 Etuto ela kanaŋ tutiya monɛ kumobe baasa la mo gbagba, mobe eche/beche 
nɛ mbia be enimu/kumu. Etuto e naa keni kanaŋ na be asheŋtirso so.
Kushuŋ
Kebɛso-kebɛso be kabaso, kabuna be enimu, kanaŋ be enimu nɛ etuto be emo 
e kɔ eleŋ achɔ mo barkasa? Delgeso kumo gberɛ ashi daŋkare be kejunkpar 
be kabaso.

KABA 7 Adaŋkare be Kawɔrɔ nɛ Daŋkare be Kejunkpar (Kewuraji)
Daŋkare be kejunkpar be kapɔr be tunɔ/ashuŋ
1. Kanaŋ be enimu
 Ade la kabuna be enimu be ashuŋ ko nna:
a. Mo ela kabuna na be demujipo.
b. Mo e naa kuŋ kabuna na be adrasheŋ.
c. Mo e naa kata kabuna na be adaŋkaresheŋ.
d.  Mo e naa kuŋ kabuna na be adaŋkaresawule.
e. Mo e naa keniso nɛ mbifolbi monɛ baa daŋ na bee bunyaŋ kanaŋ na be 
ataada.
2. Kanaŋ be kumu/enimu
 Kanaŋ be enimu bee shuŋ ashuŋ damta nɛ amobe ako la:
a. E bee kuŋ kanaŋ na ashi kprekpre nko tɔrɔ to.
b. E bee chɛto a bra kanaŋ na be nkilgi nko kebawɔtɔ lɛla.
c. A chɛto nɛ kayurwushi bee wɔ kanaŋ to.
d. E bee keni kanaŋ be kapitɛ so fanɛ kasawule, alaŋ nɛ adamta.
e. E bee yulwe lanto nawule nko lantoebi nɛ kowoebi be kɔnɔgberge.
f. A junkpar a yili kanaŋ na be eyilikpa ashi efuli na be ademu to.
g. E bee sa kanaŋebi na lakal nɛ kasheŋnyi.
h. E bee yili kanaŋ na be ayato a pɛ nkre kpra.
3.  Etuto
 Ashuŋ damta nɛ etuto bee shuŋ ashi kanaŋ to. Amobe ako ela:
a. E bee nase mbra nna n saa shinɛ a bee shuŋ.
b. Mo e naa kuŋ kanaŋ na nɛ baasa/asheŋ lubi.
c. E bee bra kanaŋ to be ndaŋ nɛ eleŋ nna.
d. E bee shuŋ fanɛ eŋinipo nna.
e. Mo e naa fin kanaŋ na be asheŋtirso a sa bumo.
Kushuŋ 7.1
Buwito kabuna be enimu be ashuŋ kpra fanɛ asa. Chige fobe atuwebi to n sa 
fo barkasa.
